books.section: Topic 6.11 Reform in the Gilded Age
Industrialization, Corporate Consolidation, and the Gospel of Wealth

primary_sources: Coxey’s Army photograph, 1894; Coney Island trade card, about 1885–1896

stimulus.text: Image 1: An 1894 photograph shows a column of men marching down a dirt road toward Washington, carrying banners. One banner reads “More Money! Less Misery! Good Roads!” A placard shows a portrait with the words “Death to Interest on Bonds.” The caption reads “Coxey’s Army approaching Washington.” Image 2: A color trade card from about 1885–1896, “Scene at Coney Island,” shows boys in suits digging in the sand on a crowded beach, with a sailboat and a paddle steamer on the water and amusement buildings, a tall tower, and an elephant-shaped hotel behind them.
stimulus.source_note: Image 1: 1894 stereograph, Library of Congress (LC-DIG-stereo-1s09209), public domain; image viewed by the writer (shared pool: u6/original-u6-coxeys-army-approaching-washington.jpg). Image 2: chromolithograph trade card, Lindner, Eddy and Clauss, New York, about 1885-1896, public domain; image viewed by the writer (shared pool: u6/u6-coney-island-scene.jpg).

stem: What does Image 1 show about how some Americans responded to the depression of the 1890s?

options.text: They left the country to find work abroad
options.misconception: The marchers are heading toward Washington, not leaving the country.

options.text: They marched on Washington to demand federal action
They formed a new political party in Congress
options.misconception: The image shows a march, not the founding of a party.

options.text: They opened new factories in the West
options.misconception: The image shows marchers on a road, not factories.

rationales.A: The marchers are on the road to Washington, not on their way out of the country.
rationales.B: The banners demand more money and good roads, and the marchers head for the capital.
rationales.C: No party is founded in the photograph; the men are marching.
rationales.D: No factories appear in the photograph.
rationales.general:
Read the banners and the road.
1. The men march in a column down a dirt road toward Washington.
2. Their banner reads “More Money! Less Misery! Good Roads!”
3. Those are demands aimed at the federal government, not at a boss or a town.
4. Background from the books: Coxey’s Army marched in 1894, after the Panic of 1893 left millions jobless.
Remember: a march on the capital is a demand aimed at the national government.
